items.item: Why the hash map alone isn't enough: it finds an entry in O(1) but keeps no usable order, and the doubly linked list alone isn't enough either: it orders entries but needs the map to avoid an O(n) scan to find one
Why a node needing to know its own neighbours (not just its value) is what makes an O(1) splice possible, the same property the linked-list topic names
That a get is also a write: moving the touched entry to the front changes shared state on every read, not only on a put

at.step: What does a hit do, besides read?

items.item: Why that write-on-read is exactly what makes a shared LRU cache contend under many threads: the reorder needs exclusive access even for a pure lookup

items.item: That CLOCK's reference bit is a cheaper, coarser substitute for exact recency, not a free win: it gives up knowing which of several set-bit entries was used most recently, in exchange for a hit costing one bit set

at.step: What would make a hit cheaper?

items.item: Why CLOCK's measured miss ratio lands close to exact LRU's on a workload with real locality, and that the gap is a property of the workload, not a universal guarantee

Why neither LRU nor CLOCK can tell 'used once, as part of something bigger than the cache' apart from 'used constantly': both rely only on recency, which a one-pass scan satisfies for everything it touches

at.step: What happens when one giant scan runs through?

items.item: That measuring the damage of a scan requires looking at a short window right after it, not the whole recovery period, since the cache self-warms and the effect otherwise disappears into noise — a real measurement mistake this topic's own script caught and fixed
